items.summary_en: Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.
items.extracted_title: Credit Saison achieves 954% ROI in a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot
items.extracted_excerpt: Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Credit Saison achieves 954% ROI in a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption. 954% Return on investment (ROI) in the pilot 14 hours saved per pilot participant each month 1 month from the end of the pilot to the decision to roll out ChatGPT Enterprise companywide 850 hours saved per month on average through the engineering team’s use of Codex Credit Saison’s business centers on credit cards, with approximately 31.16 million cardholders. The company also operates financing and international businesses. In September 2025, Credit Saison rolled out ChatGPT Enterprise to all employees. A pilot had exceeded its targets for time savings, giving the company the confidence to approve a companywide rollout just one month after the pilot ended. The rollout gave every employee access to AI at work. That shift began with the pilot. With many employees in generalist roles, Credit Saison wanted to understand how AI could improve everyday work and deliver tangible results. Kazutoshi Ono, Credit Saison’s Senior Managing Executive Officer, CDO, and CTO, set a clear direction: “We won’t know until we really put it to work.” Working with OpenAI, the company ran a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot with 315 participants for a little over a month, from late June to early August 2025. The group brought together volunteers, employees nominated by the project team, every executive including the president, and representatives from every department. It accounted for just under 10% of the company’s approximately 3,700 employees in Japan. The results? Credit Saison reports a 954% return on investment (ROI) and 14 hours saved per employee each month, equivalent to approximately 169 hours annually. Both figures significantly exceeded the company’s initial targets of 500% ROI and 7.5 hours saved per person per month. In a survey after the pilot, 75% of managers and 70% of nonmanagerial employees said they could not do without ChatGPT Enterprise. Approximately 80% of respondents in the legal department felt it improved their ability to do their jobs, while more than 80% in the IT department reported greater job satisfaction. The benefits extended beyond time savings to how employees felt about their capabilities and their work. The pilot’s results reflected both the support in place and the people involved. Credit Saison’s CoE, which leads AI adoption, used a dedicated Slack channel to share successes and failures openly. Individual experiences became lessons the whole organization could use. OpenAI supported the effort with training for executives and practical workshops for beginners, helping participants apply AI to their work. One highlight of the pilot was a custom GPT designed to simulate shareholder meetings. Using voice mode, employees could rehearse realistic, interactive exchanges that mirrored an actual shareholder meeting. The GPT drew particularly strong interest from Credit Saison’s senior leadership, and requests to share the prompt soon followed. This enthusiasm helped drive broader adoption of voice-based AI across the company. Leadership’s engagement went beyond showing interest. Ono encouraged Katsumi Mizuno, Credit Saison’s representative director, executive president and COO, to lead by example: “It’s not enough to encourage employees to use it. Leaders need to use it regularly themselves.” Mizuno embraced this approach, creating his own custom GPT for company research and incorporating it into his daily work. Executives were using AI themselves while employees were finding practical applications. Together, those efforts connected the decision to invest with everyday use, helping Credit Saison approve a companywide rollout within a month of completing the pilot. Across Credit Saison, employees are finding practical ways to incorporate ChatGPT into their everyday work, as these three use cases illustrate. Retail sales: capturing daily team debriefs - At counters in shopping malls and other locations, Credit Saison employees help customers sign up for and use credit cards. A custom GPT for store performance reporting helps these teams document their meetings at the end of each day. - Using audio from the regular debrief, the GPT automatically summarizes each employee’s results, meeting notes, handover items for the next day, and areas to focus on. Teams keep running their meetings as usual while spending less time on documentation and compiling results. The familiar workflow makes it easy to adopt even for employees new to AI, and it is now used at every location. Corporate sales: turning business challenges into better proposals - Corporate sales teams use a custom GPT for company research to analyze customers. It helps them identify business challenges and assess where Credit Saison’s services could help. - In one company analysis, it surfaced challenges that employees themselves had not fully recognized. By streamlining research and analysis before sales meetings, the GPT is helping teams improve the quality of their proposals. Inside sales: giving new hires more opportunities to practice - Inside sales teams needed to give less experienced employees more opportunities to practice without taking experienced colleagues away from selling. - A custom GPT for prospect roleplay helps address that challenge. The AI plays the prospective customer, allowing employees to rehearse sales conversations by voice and receive feedback afterward. Teams value the chance to gain practical experience before speaking with real prospects. Results at a glance - 954% ROI achieved in a pilot with 315 participants - 14 hours saved per participant per month, equivalent to approximately 169 hours a year - 75% of managers and 70% of nonmanagerial employees said they could not do without ChatGPT Enterprise in the post-pilot survey - Approximately 80% of legal department respondents reported an improved ability to do their jobs, and more than 80% of IT department respondents reported greater job satisfaction in the same survey - A decision to roll out ChatGPT Enterprise companywide within one month of completing the pilot Credit Saison sees AI transformation, or AX, as having three dimensions. The first, “Employee AX,” changes how employees work and enables things they could not have done without AI. That extends beyond the use of ChatGPT in sales. In engineering, for example, Credit Saison reports that Codex saves an average of 850 hours of work each month. The company is also looking toward “Customer AX,” which focuses on improving customer experiences, user interfaces, and user experience, and “Corporate AX,” which rethinks organizational structures and roles around AI. For Customer AX, Credit Saison is developing an AI call center in-house. Corporate AX is at an earlier stage, with the company identifying specific applications. items.summary_en: OpenAI will honor a shared robots.txt signal to help website operators communicate their AI training preferences to participating providers.
items.extracted_title: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI will honor a shared robots.txt signal to help website operators communicate their AI training preferences to participating providers.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Today, we’re announcing that OpenAI will honor a common signal(opens in a new window) in robots.txt, the file that lets websites express their preferences about the use of their content for foundational generative AI training. This voluntary effort makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once. Previously, website operators would identify individual crawlers and maintain separate rules for each and every provider. Having a shared signal across multiple providers reduces that work for operators. We aim to implement the signal in the coming months, and will share another update with details about our implementation when we do so. This new signal will not replace the controls we already provide through robots.txt. Our existing crawler controls(opens in a new window), which provide web publishers flexibility and control over their pages, will continue to apply and be respected. This draws on the ongoing work(opens in a new window) of the Internet Engineering Task Force’s (IETF) AI Preferences working group. We’re joining other participants in the working group in today’s announcement of this shared signal, and believe this strengthens our continued participation in the IETF standards discussions. OpenAI will continue to adapt its practices as those conversations and the landscape continue to evolve in view of appropriate controls and fairness. We believe this is a practical step toward an open web where people can publish and discover information, and website owners have clearer, simpler ways to communicate their choices about how their content is used. We encourage other AI providers to honor the signal.

items.summary_en: OpenAI is strengthening violence prevention in ChatGPT with expanded safeguards, earlier interventions, and a new commitment to public safety reporting.
items.extracted_title: Community safety report and new protections for teens
items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI is strengthening violence prevention in ChatGPT with expanded safeguards, earlier interventions, and a new commitment to public safety reporting.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: ChatGPT is one of the world’s most widely used AI products, and we have invested in building some of the industry’s most advanced systems for detecting potential harm, reviewing concerning activity, and escalating credible threats. We’re making two announcements to further our work in this area: a new Community Safeguards Report and more restrictions around firearms content for minors. Keeping communities safe continues to be a top priority for OpenAI. Our work includes bringing imminent threats of violence to the attention of law enforcement, and we made over 200 law enforcement referrals in Q3 2026. These referrals are making a positive(opens in a new window) difference(opens in a new window) in disrupting violent plots, and we continue to rely on mental health and behavioral experts to help us assess difficult cases. We recognize AI companies have a distinct role to play alongside law enforcement, family members, mental-health professionals, and policymakers, who bring critical authority, context and real-world reach. We are committed to making the most of that role by continuously strengthening our systems, sharing what we learn, and working directly with those who are best positioned to act in the real world. We are constantly strengthening the steps we take to help protect people and communities. That means building strong safeguards, and also being transparent about how well they work and what we’re doing to enhance them. We want to give people a clear picture of our approach, how our models identify and respond to harmful behavior, the risks we see in practice, and the steps we take to address them. We’re committing to launch the Community Safety Report on violence prevention and other community safety issues, and the effectiveness of our safeguards. The report will explain how we train our systems to detect, investigate, and respond to community safety issues. We’ll share anonymized examples of how violence-related harm manifests and what we’re learning, highlight new mitigations and policy changes, and include relevant data to support these findings. We will publish our first report in early 2027, covering the second half of 2026, with updates every six months thereafter. Our commitment is to share meaningful findings about how we identify, review, and respond to potentially harmful content. Our models are trained to not give instructions that would help someone plan or carry out violence. We’re now placing additional restrictions on how ChatGPT responds to questions about past mass attacks and the people who carried them out, directing the model to provide less detailed information in those areas even if it is available from other online sources. People should be able to ask ChatGPT to help them understand these events, how victims and communities were impacted, and learn about recognizing warning signs and preventing future violence. But we’re tightening our policies to restrict reconstructions of past mass attacks, including details about the weapons and equipment used and how they were obtained, and detailed comparisons on scale of harm that could amplify an attacker’s notoriety. These limits apply regardless of a user’s age or reason for asking. Sometimes a request that seems ordinary on its own takes on a different meaning in light of an earlier conversation. In May, we shared how ChatGPT can use short, factual summaries of earlier warning signs to respond more carefully in a later chat. We’re building on that work so that when recent chats show warning signs of possible violence, ChatGPT will respond more conservatively when sharing information that could be misused. We’re also working to apply those stricter limits when we predict someone is under 18, even if their chats show no signs of violent intent. We ban accounts that we determine have violated our policies on violent activity. We’re also working with mental health and violence prevention experts on additional, automated ways to intervene earlier. When a conversation shows signs that someone is fixating on violence or the idea of seriously harming another person, ChatGPT will be able to automatically end the chat to interrupt that pattern in the moment. If ChatGPT ends multiple chats for that reason, we may temporarily pause the account. This is an ongoing effort and we continue to strengthen and invest in technical and practical protections, including how to recognize warning signs reliably and determine when and how to intervene. ChatGPT for Teens applies age-appropriate safeguards for users under 18, with stronger protections and additional limits to reduce exposure to sensitive content. We’re now placing further limits on weapons-related information teens can receive, even when a question appears harmless. Our policies already prohibit helping anyone plan or carry out violence and restrict helping teens find or obtain weapons. We’re extending those protections to restrict practical information about weapons and security systems that could be misused to facilitate violence, even when there’s no sign of violent intent. Teens can still use ChatGPT to help prevent and de-escalate violence, seek support, and connect with a trusted adult. We launched age prediction last year, which analyzes multiple signals such as behavior patterns to estimate whether a user may be under or over 18. We strengthened our age prediction system to continually assess new signals as people use ChatGPT and move teens into the under 18 experience when appropriate. Users who are incorrectly placed in the under 18 experience will always have a fast, privacy-protective way to confirm they are adults and have additional teen protections removed through Persona, our age verification partner. Our parental controls let parents link their ChatGPT accounts to their teens and manage safety settings together. Linked accounts include safety alerts that may be sent when specially trained reviewers identify a serious self-harm concern and behaviors that may be associated with disordered eating. In July, we expanded those alerts to notify parents if their teen’s account has been deactivated for violating our usage policies on violence. We are working to introduce notifications for parents if we pause their teen’s account for repeatedly discussing violence, as detailed above. Acts of real-world violence are heartbreaking and complex, with many contributing factors. They are also a stark reminder that we must continue designing and iterating our systems to account for the inherently complicated realities of human behavior. Developing effective violence safeguards in AI systems requires solving novel problems in recognizing risk and responding appropriately, and we will continue to invest in, iterate, and share learnings on how best to implement the protections we’re pursuing. The safeguards detailed here will begin rolling out in the next few weeks and we will continue to refine them. We remain committed to mitigating risks of harm in

items.title: Fair use benefits everyone
items.summary_zh: OpenAI 更新了模型或产品能力更新，关键在于模型能力、部署成本、权限控制或开发者工作流的实际变化。
items.summary_en: OpenAI shares excerpts from court briefs by creators, academics, accessibility advocates, and legal experts, among others, on how fair use supports AI training and innovation.
items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI shares excerpts from court briefs by creators, academics, accessibility advocates, and legal experts, among others, on how fair use supports AI training and innovation.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Fair use benefits everyone Authors, journalists, creators, academics, accessibility advocates, legal experts, librarians, economists and business leaders are voicing their support for the longstanding principle of fair use and its application to AI training. For decades, fair use has played a critical role in driving innovation that benefits everyone. It has helped deliver important medical and scientific breakthroughs and new technologies that have made real and positive differences for countless people, including authors and journalists. The New York Times’ lawsuit, meanwhile, asks everyone to ignore a half century of legal history and progress, and toss aside the longstanding principle of fair use in their own narrow pursuit of an undeserved payday. Experts and leaders across a wide range of fields have recognized that fair use is a win-win that benefits everyone, and have shared their perspectives with the Court in filing briefs in support of fair use. Below you’ll find excerpts from some of those submissions, in their own words. The full filings are available on the public court docket, and you can read more about fair use and AI here. - AI Progress - American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance - Authors Alliance - Engine and Developers Alliance - Foundation for American Innovation - Joshua S. Gans - Kevin Kelly - Matthew Sag - Michael Wall and Sarah Rose Siskind - Public Knowledge - Ron Suskind and Brian L. Frye - United States Government AI Progress The Court should reject Plaintiffs’ attempt to extend copyright beyond its established limits. AI training uses copyrighted works for a fundamentally different purpose, does not provide the public with substitute access to those works, and does not cause the market harm cognizable under the Copyright Act. Instead, it enables a broad array of transformative technologies that are already delivering public benefits. Copyright exists to promote creativity and progress, not to suppress lawful innovation or protect authors from competition. Settled fair use principles therefore compel the conclusion that generative AI training is fair use. American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance This case concerns more than companies that develop large language models (LLMs). It affects medical researchers and patients, educators serving students with different learning needs, people with disabilities seeking greater independence, farmers applying agricultural knowledge, independent creators developing new forms of expression, and industry sectors from software to the law. These communities share an interest in the ability to study and learn from broad and diverse sources of knowledge, and in access to the tools that make that learning useful. Many depend on systems developed by others, including open source AI systems, rather than training models themselves. Fair use supports their ability to learn, discover, communicate, and create. Restrictions on fair use training would affect both the institutions building AI and the people using it. Authors Alliance The market dilution theory asks copyright law to protect rightsholders against an economic phenomenon that it has never restricted before. New works can reduce the sales, visibility, or value of older works without copying their protected expression. The Copyright Act deliberately leaves that competition outside the copyright owner’s control. Amicus therefore respectfully asks the Court to hold that “market dilution,” i.e., aggregate competitive pressure from noninfringing outputs, including those that occupy the same subject matter or genre, that share unprotected characteristics, or compete for the same audience, is not cognizable market harm under 17 U.S.C. § 107(4). Rejecting the theory would preserve the distinction the Second Circuit has always maintained: copyright protects authors against substitution for their protected expression, not against the success of new expression that merely competes with it. Engine and Developers Alliance Startups’ use of foundation models demonstrates that using copyrighted works to train an AI model is a fair use, not copyright infringement. The purpose of training a foundation model is not to reproduce the works it learns; it is to build a general-purpose tool that others can adapt to new ends. The ends startups have chosen bear no resemblance to the purposes of the works in any training dataset. Foundation for American Innovation To the extent AI training enables the creation of new knowledge, expression, software, and other capabilities, those benefits bear on factor four’s assessment of the use’s market effects. That reasoning supports a novel application here: considering the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis, software, and other productive work. Joshua S. Gans Professor of Strategic Management Copyright supports not only the incentive to create content but also the incentive to build tools that learn from that content, and a rule that treated every displaced sale as actionable can weaken the second without reliably protecting the first. Kevin Kelly Author AI is a transformative technology that accelerates the creation of novel works across countless disciplines in the arts and sciences. Mr. Kelly has experience in how AI advances the field of literature. In his view, each AI model can be understood as an entirely new medium that offers authors the capability to create new texts and ideas, and to reason. A ruling for Plaintiffs on fair use would therefore grant Plaintiffs far more than the limited monopoly to their original expression Congress intended to confer. It would hinder the development of technologies capable of disseminating previously unimaginable quantities of information. It would also impede new modes of thought and the creation of new original works in both the arts and sciences. Amicus files this brief in support of Defendants’ argument that the use of copyrighted works to train large language models is a fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. Based on his lifelong pursuits of writing, the protections afforded to copyright owners are important to Mr. Kelly. Equally vital is preserving room for permissible uses of copyrighted material and the growth of transformative technologies. Otherwise, copyright will stifle the very creativity, innovation, and spread of knowledge it exists to encourage. The fair-use doctrine is critical to ensuring that balance. Matthew Sag Professor of Law On the record in this case, the defendants’ use of plaintiffs’ works for AI training is highly transformative and strongly favors a finding of fair use because under realistic conditions the outputs of defendants’ models are in no relevant way similar to the invisible intermediate copies made during the

items.extracted_title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
items.extracted_excerpt: Scientists at the Allen Telescope Array have integrated the NVIDIA Holoscan platform to search for signals that may come from aliens — or the AI they built.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI, a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther, a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS. Nexus, a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument. Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours. Science Fact, Not Fiction The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula. Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon. Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science.

items.title: nemotron-halloween
items.summary_zh: Hugging Face Blog 更新了模型或产品能力更新，关键在于模型能力、部署成本、权限控制或开发者工作流的实际变化。
items.summary_en: Hugging Face Blog has an AI update relevant to product, industry or technical direction.
items.extracted_excerpt: A Blog post by NVIDIA on Hugging Face
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Or rather… TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation. I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain. That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk. - Listening: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 ASR turns visitor speech into text. [nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b.q8_0.gguf ] - Thinking: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open small language model for conversational agents, writes each reply. A LoRA adapter supplies the personality. - Speaking: NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot voices each reply from a short reference sample of the character. - Animating: NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D turns clean speech into mouth animation in Unreal Engine 5. - Seeing: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni describes costumes, while YOLO and ByteTrack count and track visitors. - Running it: NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent coordinates everything on one workstation with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors. A few expressions from a house with plenty to say. Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster. While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about. The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it. The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice. Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget. The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline. After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison. If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B. It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply. Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship. Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job. With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not. Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects. A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing. median end-of-speech-to-audio with Bolt Q4 & TTS = 1.70 seconds median end-of-speech-to-audio cached responses = 0.72 seconds (note: speech-end detection currently waits for 300 ms of silence ) NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice”
